content: A specialized antenatal education program aimed at teaching women to recognize the onset of active labor may provide several benefits. These include potentially reducing the frequency of early hospital admissions, enhancing women's confidence, fostering a sense of control and empowerment, and alleviating anxiety. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the impact of teaching pregnant women specific criteria to self-diagnose the onset of active labor at term. The Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register was searched in October 2007, and the search was updated on November 30, 2012. The results of the updated search were added to the awaiting classification section of the review. The review included randomized trials that compared a structured antenatal education intervention for identifying symptoms of active labor with standard care. The quality of the trials was assessed. One study, involving 245 women, met the inclusion criteria. However, the method of randomization in this study was unclear, and 15% of the participants were lost to follow-up. The study found that a specific antenatal education program was associated with a reduction in the average number of visits to the labor suite before the onset of active labor. The weighted mean difference was -0.29, with a 95% confidence interval ranging from -0.47 to -0.11. However, it remains uncertain whether this reduction in visits led to fewer women being sent home because they were not in active labor. The authors concluded that there is insufficient evidence to determine the effectiveness of using a specific set of criteria for self-diagnosing the onset of active labor.
